vignette: Aris sits on the edge of the cushioned chair, his forearms resting on his knees, fingers tracing the same frayed thread on the upholstery. He is twenty-six, with the quiet posture of someone who has learned to take up less space. The office is familiar to him now, but his shoulders remain tight, caught in a braced position that never quite relaxes. He works as a bank teller, a job he chose for its predictability, yet predictability has become the very thing that haunts him. Three years ago, the blast tears through a night market in his home province. He is standing in line, waiting for tea, when the world fractures into sound and heat. The memory does not stay buried; it arrives in fragments. A sudden hiss of a coffee machine at work pulls him back to the screech of twisted metal. A man in a heavy coat reminds him of the silhouette that vanished into the smoke. He tells me he still wakes at 3 a.m., not from a dream, but from the phantom sensation of glass settling over his skin. He checks the deadbolt twice before sleeping, then again when he rises. In his community, grief is meant to be shared, but he has found it easier to carry his alone. At the bank, Aris stands behind the tempered glass, counting cash with mechanical precision. Customers ask for deposits, withdrawals, loan information, and his responses are correct, measured, almost clinical. But his eyes never rest on one face for more than a few seconds. He watches the doors, the corners, the hands. When a car backfires outside, his pen skids across the ledger, and for a moment, the teller window feels impossibly thin. He tells me he starts wearing noise-canceling earbuds during his commute, then stops when his manager notices. Now he simply sits in his car for twenty minutes after parking, breathing through a count that always stops at four. He cannot explain why it has to be four. His marriage lasts two years and ends last winter. He does not blame the trauma directly, but he describes the distance as a wall that grows between them, quiet and inevitable. His partner stops asking where he is when he checks the street from the balcony, when he cancels dinner plans because a news alert flickers on his phone, when he no longer sleeps in the same bed. Aris says he still loves her, but love feels like a heavy coat he can no longer carry. He keeps her side of the closet untouched, not as a shrine, but because moving anything feels like disturbing a site he cannot bear to revisit. In session, Aris speaks in a steady, low voice, yet his breath hitches when he describes the approaching anniversary. He tells me he feels like a building that survives a quake but now flinches at the wind. He avoids the news, cancels flights, and has stopped driving through tunnels. His friends drift away, not from malice, but because his presence becomes a quiet gravity, pulling conversations toward caution and away from celebration. He knows his reactions feel “too much,” as his mother once sighs, but he cannot tell the difference between a warning and a memory. He wonders if the tension in his jaw will ever loosen, or if it has simply become his new face. He leans forward now, pressing his palms flat against his thighs, as if grounding himself in the room. The clock ticks. Outside, a siren passes, faint and distant. Aris does not startle. He exhales slowly, watches his breath fog the air for a second, then looks up. He is still here. He is still counting. He is still waiting for the moment his body finally believes the world is safe enough to stop bracing.
